newsitem.title: UK: British shares end firmer as cash keeps flowing.
newsitem.headline: British shares end firmer as cash keeps flowing.

text.p: Leading British shares ended broadly higher on Monday as investors shrugged off last Friday's 88 point slide, hoping that a tidal wave of institutional funds will continue to keep the market afloat.

A robust early performance by U.S. stocks and continuing evidence that institutional investors on both sides of the Atlantic are still awash with cash helped push the Financial Times Index of 100 leading shares 48.6 points higher to close at 4,011.6.
"You cannot go against the huge amount of institutional funds coming into this market," the head of trading at a major investment bank said.
"Until the host of share buy-backs and special dividends dries up causing fund inflows to abate, share prices are going to remain at these ridiculously high levels," he added.

British pension funds and insurance companies, which invest thousands of millions of pounds in the London share market, have been flush with cash this year as many British companies have paid out hefty dividends or bought back their own shares.
Companies sometimes initiate buy-backs with spare cash in order to reduce the number of shares in circulation, which enhances shareholder value.

Trading volume was a meagre 490 million shares compared with an average daily volume of 760 million in the previous four sessions, reflecting the market's overall wariness of a Wall Street which has jumped nearly 28 percent, or over 1,300 points, so far this year.
"Generally the optimism seems to be hardening that we are not at the start of some sort of meltdown," said the head of equity sales at a large brokerage house.
"We do expect there to be a further significant setback in the markets in coming months, but we also believe we may not have seen the highs yet," he added.

British investors were also jittery folowing the latest outbreak of hostilities in the ruling Conservative party. "Euro-sceptic" members of parliament on Monday called a news conference after Prime Minister John Major in a weekend television interview said he would not be bullied over policy towards the European Union.
Some leading euro-sceptics last week called for the sacking of finance minister Kenneth Clarke after he refused to rule out joining the planned European single currency.
"Monetary union and the prospect of a single currency is an issue," said Andy Hartwill, shares strategist at stockbrokers SGST Strauss Turnbull.
"The divisiveness of the issue is defintely weighing on the market."
The Dow industrials average, which plunged 140 points last week, was up 42 points by the London close, as bargain hunters piled into selective issues, dealers said.
Firm bond markets also helped share prices, they said.

The March long gilt future ended 23/32 higher at 109-20/32, cheered by news that one measure of inflation, UK November producer output prices, were unchanged from the previous month. The market had expected output prices to rise by 0.1 percent during the month.

Dealers said investors were now looking ahead to this week's monetary policy meeting between Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George, though George doused rate fears last week by saying he did not see an urgent need for a dramatic rate rise.
